Generally, path reconstruction is a best-effort approach. The result of the taint propagation phase is a taint graph that connects sources to sinks via data flow edges. FlowDroid then starts at the sinks and traverses the graph backwards to generate paths between sources and sinks. Unfortunately, taint graphs can contain cycles (loops, recursions). Therefore, the number of paths between a given source and a given sink is unbounded in the general case. FlowDroid solves this issue by returning a "witness", i.e., one path among all that are possible for a given pair of source and sink. This process is relatively complex, so  I suspect some paths get dropped here.

Infer is not deterministic

Infer analysis has some heuristics on when to give up.  These metrics are somehow time based or otherwise impacted by the load or compute power of a system.  As a result, some runs can detect bugs that other runs miss, even on the same code using the same version of infer.

For example:

```

$ git clone https://github.com/TomMD/s2n
$ cd s2n
$ git checkout origin/pr1075-dst
$ cmake . -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=1
$ infer capture --compilation-database compile_commands.json
$ infer analyze
...
Summary of the reports

          MEMORY_LEAK: 9
  UNINITIALIZED_VALUE: 3
           DEAD_STORE: 3
        RESOURCE_LEAK: 2
```

Is there a mechanism, or understood development path to implement a mechanism, which can make infer fully deterministic but still have reasonable performance and the ability to give up on an analysis?

There are many contributing factors to infer's non-determinism, some more fundamental than others.

## Analysis scheduling and mutually-recursive functions

During the analysis of mutually-recursive procedures, the following happens: say `f()` calls `g()` calls `h()` calls `f()`, and infer starts analysing `f`. It will need to summarise `g` first, so it pauses the analysis of `f` and starts analysing `g` instead. This happens in [`Ondemand.analyze_proc_name`](https://github.com/facebook/infer/blob/007c044d92917afc86cfbf54d521bf45b88cd182/infer/src/backend/ondemand.ml#L286-L288). Notice in particular that this module maintains a list of "active procedures" which for now contains `f` and `g`. Then the same thing happens for `h`, then infer asks for the summary for `f` again. At that point, the active procedures are `f`, `g`, and `h`, so since `f` active ondemand will break the cycle by returning an empty summary.

Depending on which procedure this process starts with, you'll get different analysis results. Here `h` was analysed assuming an empty summary for `f`, but if we'd started at `g` then some summary for `f` would have been computed (assuming an empty summary for `g`) and the summary for `h` would thus probably have been different.

Infer's way of resolving mutual recursion is particularly crude here. It is standard to try and reach a fixpoint for instance. However that usually still results in non-determinism because of widening.

## Parallelism

Parallelism makes the problem of mutually-recursive procedures worse because it will randomise which procedure we start the analysis from in the cycles. Disabling parallelism usually reduces non-determinism significantly/completely.

## Biabduction timeouts

This is specific to the biabduction analysis in infer: there's a hard limit of wall clock time after which the analysis of a procedure is stopped. You can disable this by setting `--seconds-per-iteration` very high (or adding an option to disable these entirely... beware that the biabduction analysis might not terminate. However there's also a "symbolic" timeout that counts the number of symbolic operations performed. That might influence non-determinism but probably not or not as badly). This is set [here](https://github.com/facebook/infer/blob/007c044d92917afc86cfbf54d521bf45b88cd182/infer/src/base/Config.ml#L2530).



PS: this list is probably not exhaustive... for instance, we also do bug deduplication at various levels and while we try to do so deterministically your mileage may vary.

Some more actionable comments.

Actually, the list of sources of non-determinism above might well be exhaustive, though I wouldn't bet my life on it.

We have some thoughts floating around for attacking the issue of recursion which you might find interesting: one could imagine trying to discover the parts of the call graph that participate in mutual recursion and then scheduling the analysis of the mutually-recursive procedures in some fixed order (alphabetically, ...).

The main complication is that computing the static "direct" call graph is easy; we do it [here](https://github.com/facebook/infer/blob/fc6aee2d064b7b1cc9ebd21338bec8abacfac92a/infer/src/backend/CallGraph.ml#L154). However, that call graph is a lie: the "analysis" call graph of "analysis of procedure X requires summary of procedure Y" might look quite different (it will likely have more procedures, eg due to dynamic dispatch or checkers looking up seemingly unrelated summaries) and is the one we actually care about for scheduling the analysis. Maybe the direct call graph is still good enough though, it would be interesting to  try. Currently we use the direct call graph to schedule the analysis of all procedures *not* in a mutual recursion cycle, so one would have to make it schedule procedures in cycles too.

Someone in our team is working on computing the analysis call graph and storing that in summaries, but that will only be available once an analysis has been performed. One could imagine storing that somewhere to make future analyses (of the same source code, so perhaps useless) deterministic, by recording also the order in which the procedures have been analysed somehow (or maybe deducing that information from what's already available, or...). That could be enough to make the analysis of code changes deterministic for instance, if that's a use case you care about.

I'd just like to say I reflect back on this information periodically as I try to find someone or time to do this work.  Work done or not, your input is very much appreciated.

[inferbo] Evaluate cpp vector parameter symbolically

Summary:
This diff evaluates a cpp vector given as a parameter symbolically. Especially, it addresses it as an array, so the cost checker can use its symbolic length correctly.

**About handling `cpp.vector_elem` field:**

The field is a virtual field of vector object that points to the array of vector elements. It was introduced in Inferbo to model semantics of vector operations.
Since many semantics of Inferbo depends on type information, it had collected type information of vector elements, whenever `cpp.vector_elem` field was introduced, as a *side-effect*. A problem is that it has *side-effect*, which means it may introduce non-deterministic analysis results depending on the type information of the virtual field.

This diff changes it not to collect the type information on `cpp.vector_elem` as a side-effect. Instead, it tries to write the information to the abstract states (abstract location) when possible.

[biabduction] specialise java models without non-determinism

Summary:
Dynamic dispatch in java requires specialisation of models. Models do not have a CFG, nor attributes, in the capture DB, so the solution til now was to get those from the summary of the model.

Each code path (CFG, attributes) could introduce non-determinism by allowing summaries to mask functions in the capture DB, and doing so depending on race conditions of the analysis (whether a summary has been written or not), as well as by the fact that CFGs from the capture DB are not pre-analysed, while summary CFGs are.

This diff eliminates both code path usages in specialisation by strictly separating functions into captured functions and models. Other summaries are never consulted, and thus cannot introduce non-determinism through timing.

NB model specialisation for clang models has been disabled in the past.

[racerd] eliminate dep cycles from attributes

Summary:
In order to silence reports on (dynamically typed/initialised) synchronised containers, RacerD processes the summary of the class initialiser and of every constructor, which contain information on container type initialisation.

Because this happens at the procedure analysis level of every method, this creates a non-call dependency which sometimes leads to dependency cycles, eg in Enums, the class initialiser calls a constructor. These cycles introduce non-determinism due to the (non)-handling of recursion.

This diff removes that analysis dependency by accumulating all containers accesses in a method summary (as if there are no synchronised container) and then at the file analysis level filters that summary given those of the class initialiser and constructors (which have already been analysed at the procedure level).

Summary:
`AnalysisCallbacks.proc_resolve_attributes` introduces non-determinism because it first looks for the attributes in a (procdesc in a) summary and if it doesn't find it then returns the value in the attribute column from the capture DB.

- the two proc descs are generally different, as the one in the summary is preanalysed and the one in the capture DB is not;
- this extends to the attributes included in the proc desc in some cases.

The plan is to eliminate these calls one by one, replacing with `Attributes.load` which only looks at the capture DB attribute column.

[ConfigImpact] Join unchecked callees from methods with the same hash

Summary:
Before this diff, when there are multiple methods with the same hash, we took one of them that had the biggest unchanged callees set and used it in differential, representing the others.  However, we found this introduces non-deterministic FPs, e.g.

* when there are multiple methods with the same size of unchanged callees, it will take one of them non-deterministically,
* when code changes resulted in changing the method with the biggest unchanged callees, it will compare two totally different methods.

To avoid the non-determinism, this diff joins all unchecked callees of methods with the same hash, instead of taking one of them arbitrarily.

Nondeterminism in FastHierarchy with phantom classes

The FastHierarchy uses intervals to efficiently represent subclassing relationships. When the FH is created, these intervals are computed by walking type hierarchy from Object, where the object interval begins at 0. Then, for each phantom class, FH walks those classes' type hierarchies to compute the intervals, again beginning at 0. Depending on the order classes are iterated, certain phantom classes can be assigned intervals that just happen to be subranges of intervals assigned to non-phantom classes. Across differnet runs, FH can nondeterministically and spuriously declare two classes subtypes of one another.

I'm not sure how to fix this bug. The easy solution would be to start each phantom classes' interval from the upper bound of the previous hierarchy's interval, but this is technically unsound as phantom classes may very well be subtypes of non-phantom classes.

Make the UnconditionalBranchFolder class stateless to avoid concurrency issues

In issue #1336 we reported a `NullPointerException` that appears sporadically as part of a race condition and that we have a created a bugfix (Pull Request) for:

```java
java.lang.NullPointerException
	at soot.jimple.toolkits.scalar.UnconditionalBranchFolder.internalTransform(UnconditionalBranchFolder.java:74)
	at soot.BodyTransformer.transform(BodyTransformer.java:51)
	at soot.Transform.apply(Transform.java:120)
	at soot.BodyPack.internalApply(BodyPack.java:50)
	at soot.Pack.apply(Pack.java:125)
	at soot.PackManager.runBodyPacks(PackManager.java:1009)
	at soot.PackManager.lambda$runBodyPacks$0(PackManager.java:660)
	at java.base/java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1128)
	at java.base/java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker.run(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:628)
	at java.base/java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:834)
```

### Problem
In our understanding (which might be wrong), it could happen that the same instance of the class `UnconditionalBranchFolder` is used by multiple threads. It is this assumption that led us to the following bug explanation:

The class `PackManager` spawns multiple threads that perform body transformations on the JIMPLE Code and the `UnconditionalBranchFolder` is one class that is part of such a body transformation.

The `UnconditionalBranchFolder` class creates two integer arrays `numFound` and `numFixed`, which it stores as attributes. This is done on-demand, meaning that the arrays are allocated as soon as the first thread requires access to it [1].

The NullPointerException can happen if one thread already allocated the `numFound` array in line 68, but not yet the `numFixed` array in line 69:
```java
    // allocate counters once only
    if (numFound == null) {
      numFound = new int[JUMPOPT_TYPES + 1];
      numFixed = new int[JUMPOPT_TYPES + 1];
    }
```

Then, another thread skips the allocation, because the if-statement in line 67 evaluates to `false` and as `numFixed` is still `null`, it runs into a null pointer access in line 74.

There are other race-conditions possible, but they currently stay unobserved. For example, it could be that one thread started to store values into such array in the for loop, but in the meantime the array is reassigned by another thread, so that the calculated values until that point are lost and the analysis continues on invalid data.

Therefore we decided to not use attributes in this case, but to have each execution of the `internalTransform()` method to operate on its own datastructure.

[1] https://github.com/Sable/soot/blob/master/src/main/java/soot/jimple/toolkits/scalar/UnconditionalBranchFolder.java#L66

### Our solution
Instead of storing the "state" in instance variables, the state is stored in local variables and passed to other methods via parameters methods as needed.
